passage: Asif sat on the verandah step of their village house with a sheet torn from his school notebook. "Amma, how do I write Happy Birthday?" His mother Chandrika wiped her hands and wrote the two words in big letters on another page. Asif put his finger under the H, looked, and copied it. Then he looked again for the A. One letter at a time. His B came out backwards, so he rubbed it out and tried again. When the last Y was done he held the card up to the evening light. "For Dadi," he said.

qa.q: Who wrote the words in big letters for Asif to copy?
qa.a: His mother Chandrika wrote them on another page.

qa.q: What might Asif be feeling as he holds the finished card up to the light?
qa.a: He is probably proud that he wrote every letter himself. He is also happy about giving it to Dadi.

qa.q: What other approach could Asif use for the spelling, and why might it work?
qa.a: He could sound out each part of the words with his mother, clapping the beats. Hearing the parts would help him choose the letters.

qa.q: How might Chandrika feel while watching Asif copy the letters?
qa.a: She may feel patient and proud. She gave him the writing he could not do yet and let him do the copying himself.

grounding: A child asks his mother how to spell the greeting and copies her letters one at a time, so the adult supplies what he cannot yet do.

passage: Chen knelt at the kitchen table in their Vancouver apartment with a blue marker and a folded card for Leila. He had drawn a dog. The words were the hard part. "Mom, how do you write Happy Birthday?" Mom wrote it in big letters on a notepad. Chen put his finger under the H. He made an H. Finger on the A. He made an A. The two Ps came out a bit wobbly. Letter by letter he got to the end, then held the card up next to Mom's page. "Same!" Mom grinned. The Y was backwards, but Leila wouldn't mind.

qa.q: What had Chen drawn on the card?
How can you tell Chen felt proud at the end?
qa.a: He held the card next to Mom's page and shouted 'Same!', which shows he felt proud and delighted to have written it himself 😊

qa.q: What else could Chen try once he knows a few more letters?
qa.a: He could sound the words out and ask Mom to check afterwards, so he leans a little less on copying each letter.

qa.q: How might Mom see the backwards Y?
qa.a: Mom grinned instead of correcting it, so she seems to care more about the effort than a perfect letter.

grounding: Shows a child asking a parent to spell a birthday greeting and copying the letters one by one from her page.

passage: The clinic waiting room was full, and Parveen's number was still far away. Ammi had brought paper and crayons. "I'll make Gopika's card," Parveen said. Gopika lived next door and her party was tomorrow. Parveen drew a balloon, then stopped. "Ammi, how do you write Happy Birthday?" Ammi wrote it slowly on the back of the clinic slip. Parveen copied the H, then looked up. Then the A. A nurse called another number; Parveen didn't even hear. By the time her own number came, every letter was on the card, and she was beaming.

qa.q: Where did Ammi write the words for Parveen?
qa.a: Ammi wrote it slowly on the back of the clinic slip.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling when every letter was on the card?
qa.a: She was beaming, so she felt happy and proud that she had written it herself.

qa.q: Which other approach could Parveen use if Ammi were busy?
qa.a: She could copy the words from a card or poster nearby, or tell the message with a picture; asking Ammi worked because Parveen can't spell it yet.

qa.q: How might the long wait look to Ammi?
qa.a: For Ammi, the card turned a slow, crowded wait into a calm, busy time for Parveen, which probably made the waiting easier.

grounding: Illustrates a child asking her mother to spell a greeting and copying it letter by letter because she cannot yet spell it.
